title: EPA Environmental Jurisdiction over Oil & Gas Operations — Overview
citation: CAA, CWA, RCRA, SDWA, EPCRA, OPA, CERCLA (40 CFR)
applies_to: Oil & gas exploration, drilling, production, gathering, processing, and support-service contractors — on Federal, tribal, state, and private lands. EPA authority is SEPARATE from BLM (mineral/surface) and OSHA (worker safety); a site can trigger all three at once.
summary: EPA administers the major federal environmental statutes that touch oil & gas sites, and most programs are delegated to authorized states (so the state agency — TCEQ in Texas, NMED in New Mexico, etc. — is usually the day-to-day permitting authority under EPA-approved rules). The core programs a field contractor meets: Clean Air Act (CAA) methane/VOC standards (NSPS OOOO/OOOOa/OOOOb, EG OOOOc); Clean Water Act (CWA) oil-spill prevention (SPCC, 40 CFR 112) and stormwater (NPDES/CGP + SWPPP); Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) Underground Injection Control (UIC) Class II wells for produced-water disposal; Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) hazardous-waste rules — with the important E&P waste exemption; EPCRA community right-to-know (Tier II inventory, TRI); Oil Pollution Act (OPA) facility response plans; and CERCLA/'sheen rule' spill reporting to the National Response Center. Origin uses this layer to answer 'what does EPA (or my delegated state) require environmentally at this site' — distinct from BLM lease stewardship and OSHA worker safety.
key_requirements: Identify which EPA programs are triggered by the site's storage, emissions, discharges, injection, and chemical inventory — then confirm whether EPA or an authorized STATE agency is the permitting authority.
Most CAA, CWA-NPDES, RCRA, and UIC programs are delegated to states; federal EPA rules set the floor and states may be stricter.
The RCRA 'E&P exemption' removes many drilling/production wastes from federal hazardous-waste rules but NOT from CAA, CWA, SDWA, OPA, DOT, or state rules.
Spill/release reporting to the National Response Center (1-800-424-8802) is immediate and is triggered by a visible sheen (oil) or a Reportable Quantity (hazardous substance) — not by permit status.
cross_refs: Methane/VOC air standards: 40 CFR 60 OOOOb/OOOOc (see epa-nsps-oooob, epa-eg-ooooc)
Produced-water injection: UIC Class II (see epa-uic-class-ii)
notes: Anchor record for the EPA layer. Reference only — never enters Origin's document send-gate. Always confirm delegated-state authority.

title: SPCC — Spill Prevention, Control, and Countermeasure Rule (40 CFR 112)
applies_to: Non-transportation-related facilities that store, use, or handle oil and could reasonably discharge oil to navigable waters or adjoining shorelines — including tank batteries, wellsites, gas plants, fuel/lube/hydraulic storage, and drilling/workover locations.
summary: The SPCC rule requires covered facilities to prepare and implement a written SPCC Plan that prevents oil from reaching navigable waters. A facility is covered if it (1) is non-transportation-related, (2) has aggregate ABOVEGROUND oil storage capacity greater than 1,320 U.S. gallons (counting only containers 55 gallons or larger) OR completely buried capacity greater than 42,000 gallons, and (3) could reasonably be expected to discharge oil to navigable waters or adjoining shorelines. Capacity — not actual contents — is what counts. The Plan must address secondary containment, inspections, integrity testing, security, training, and drainage, and must be kept at facilities normally attended at least 4 hours/day. Certification depends on size and history: a facility can SELF-CERTIFY as a 'qualified facility' if total aboveground capacity is 10,000 gallons or less and it meets the discharge-history criteria (Tier I: no single container over 5,000 gallons; Tier II: over-5,000-gallon containers allowed). Above 10,000 gallons aggregate, a licensed Professional Engineer (PE) must certify the Plan. 'Oil' is broad — crude, condensate, diesel, gasoline, lube, hydraulic, and even vegetable/animal oils.
key_requirements: Prepare and implement a written SPCC Plan BEFORE beginning operations (or amend within required timeframes for changes).
Provide secondary containment for bulk storage sized to hold the largest container plus freeboard for precipitation.
Self-certification allowed only for 'qualified facilities' (<=10,000 gal aggregate aboveground + clean discharge history); otherwise a PE must certify.
Conduct and document tank/container inspections and integrity testing; train oil-handling personnel and designate a person accountable for discharge prevention.
Review the Plan at least every 5 years and amend within 6 months of a review or whenever a facility change materially affects discharge potential.
Amend and re-certify the Plan within 6 months of any change in facility design/operation that affects discharge potential.
forms: Written SPCC Plan (no EPA form number — self-certified or PE-certified; not filed with EPA)
deadlines: SPCC Plan in place before operations begin
Report to EPA Regional Administrator within 60 days of a qualifying discharge (see epa-oil-discharge-reporting)
5-year Plan review cycle; amend within 6 months of a triggering change
penalty_structure: CWA §311 civil penalties for SPCC violations and for discharges; per-day and per-barrel penalties apply, adjusted annually for inflation. EPA can also issue administrative compliance orders.
failure_points: Assuming the rule only applies to crude — diesel/lube/hydraulic in fuel tanks and equipment counts toward the 1,320-gallon threshold.
Self-certifying a facility that is over 10,000 gallons aggregate (requires a PE) or that fails the discharge-history test.
No or undersized secondary containment; missing inspection/integrity-test records.
Letting the Plan go stale — no 5-year review, no amendment after adding tanks.
cross_refs: Facility Response Plans for larger facilities (see epa-opa-frp)
Stormwater SWPPP can cross-reference the SPCC (see epa-npdes-stormwater)
source: 40 CFR 112; epa.gov SPCC pages; SPCC Guidance for Regional Inspectors
notes: Thresholds verified: 1,320 gal aggregate aboveground (55-gal+ containers only), 42,000 gal buried, 10,000 gal self-cert ceiling, 5,000 gal Tier I single-container limit. Reference only.

title: Oil Discharge Reporting — the 'Sheen Rule' & SPCC §112.4 (40 CFR 110/112)
citation: 40 CFR Part 110 (Discharge of Oil); 40 CFR 112.4; CWA §311
applies_to: Any person in charge of a vessel or onshore/offshore facility that discharges oil to U.S. navigable waters or adjoining shorelines.
summary: The 'Discharge of Oil' regulation (40 CFR 110) — the 'sheen rule' — requires reporting of oil discharges to navigable waters or adjoining shorelines that (a) violate water-quality standards, (b) cause a film or SHEEN or discoloration on the surface, or (c) leave sludge/emulsion beneath the surface. Reporting does NOT depend on the volume spilled — a visible sheen is enough. The person in charge must notify the National Response Center (NRC) IMMEDIATELY at 1-800-424-8802 (24/7, staffed by the Coast Guard). Separately, SPCC-regulated facilities must report to the EPA Regional Administrator within 60 days when they discharge either (1) more than 1,000 gallons of oil to navigable waters in a single event, or (2) more than 42 gallons in each of two events within any 12-month period — here the gallon count is the oil that actually REACHES water, and a report to EPA is required IN ADDITION to the NRC call. NRC intake asks for reporter contact, responsible party, date/time/location, source/cause, material and quantity, and the threat posed.
key_requirements: Report ANY oil discharge that causes a sheen/film/discoloration or sludge to navigable waters immediately to the NRC at 1-800-424-8802.
Volume is irrelevant for the sheen rule — visible sheen triggers the report.
SPCC facilities: also submit written information to the EPA Regional Administrator within 60 days of a qualifying discharge (>1,000 gal single, or >42 gal in two events/12 mo reaching water).
Send a copy of the SPCC §112.4 submission to the state oil-pollution-control agency.
Follow any additional state reporting (e.g., Texas RRC/TCEQ, New Mexico OCD) — often faster deadlines.
forms: No form — telephonic NRC report; written §112.4 submission to EPA Regional Administrator
deadlines: NRC notification: immediately upon knowledge of the discharge
EPA Regional Administrator §112.4 written report: within 60 days of a qualifying discharge
penalty_structure: Failure to notify is subject to CWA §311 civil and criminal penalties; discharges themselves carry per-gallon/per-day penalties adjusted for inflation.
failure_points: Not calling the NRC because the spill 'looked small' — a sheen alone is reportable.
Calling NRC but skipping the separate SPCC §112.4 written report to EPA (and the state copy).
Missing tighter STATE reporting deadlines for produced-water/crude releases.
cross_refs: BLM also requires undesirable-event reporting on Federal leases (see blm-site-security)
source: 40 CFR 110; 40 CFR 112.4; epa.gov Oil Discharge Reporting Requirements
notes: NRC line 1-800-424-8802 verified. Reference only — never enters Origin's send-gate.

title: RCRA Oil & Gas E&P Waste Exemption (Bentsen Amendment, 40 CFR 261.4(b)(5))
applies_to: Wastes uniquely associated with the exploration, development, or production (E&P / 'primary field operations') of crude oil, natural gas, or geothermal energy.
summary: RCRA Subtitle C regulates hazardous waste from cradle to grave, but 40 CFR 261.4(b)(5) — the 'Bentsen Amendment,' backed by EPA's 1988 Regulatory Determination — EXEMPTS drilling fluids, produced waters, and other wastes uniquely associated with oil & gas E&P from federal hazardous-waste regulation. The exempt/non-exempt line turns on how the waste was generated, NOT its toxicity. Rule of thumb: if the waste came from DOWN-HOLE or was generated by contact with the production stream while removing water/contaminants from the product, it is likely EXEMPT (e.g., drilling muds, produced water, rig-wash from the production stream, tank-bottom sludge, pit sludges, produced sand, H2S/CO2 production gases). Wastes NOT uniquely associated with E&P are NON-EXEMPT and must be evaluated as hazardous (e.g., unused/waste solvents cleaning surface equipment, used oil, waste paint, spent hydraulic fluid from equipment, laboratory wastes, transportation-pipeline wastes, refinery wastes). CRITICAL: the exemption is ONLY from federal RCRA Subtitle C. Exempt wastes still must be managed properly and remain subject to RCRA Subtitle D (solid waste), state hazardous/non-hazardous rules, and CAA/CWA/SDWA/OPA/DOT.
key_requirements: Determine for each waste stream whether it is 'uniquely associated' with E&P (exempt) or not (non-exempt) — document the determination.
Down-hole origin or contact with the production stream (removing water/contaminants) = likely exempt.
Surface solvents, used oil, shop chemicals, and transportation-pipeline wastes are generally NON-exempt — evaluate under RCRA generator rules.
Manage exempt wastes properly anyway — the exemption does not mean the waste is harmless, and state/Subtitle D rules still apply.
Never assume 'everything on an E&P site is exempt' — it is waste-by-waste.
failure_points: Treating solvents, used oil, or shop chemicals as exempt because they are on an oil site — they are usually non-exempt.
Ignoring state rules — many states regulate exempt E&P wastes more strictly (pits, NORM, produced water).
Mixing a non-exempt hazardous waste with an exempt stream and assuming the mixture stays exempt.
Forgetting that transportation-pipeline and refinery wastes fall OUTSIDE the exemption.
source: 40 CFR 261.4(b)(5); EPA 'Exemption of Oil and Gas E&P Wastes from Federal Hazardous Waste Regulations'; 1988 Regulatory Determination (53 FR 25446)
notes: Reference only. The exemption is federal-RCRA-Subtitle-C only; state and other-statute obligations persist.

title: RCRA Hazardous Waste Generator Categories (VSQG / SQG / LQG, 40 CFR 262)
applies_to: Any oil & gas contractor that generates NON-exempt hazardous waste — solvents, used oil that fails, spent shop chemicals, waste paint, contaminated absorbents, lab waste, etc.
summary: For wastes that are NOT covered by the E&P exemption, RCRA sorts generators into three categories by monthly quantity, and the rules scale up with volume. Very Small Quantity Generator (VSQG): <=100 kg/month hazardous waste (and <=1 kg/month acute); minimal requirements. Small Quantity Generator (SQG): >100 to <1,000 kg/month; needs an EPA ID number, may accumulate up to 180 days (or 270 if shipping >200 miles), basic training/emergency contacts. Large Quantity Generator (LQG): >=1,000 kg/month (or >1 kg/month acute); EPA ID, 90-day accumulation limit, full contingency plan, personnel training, biennial report. All generators must make an accurate hazardous-waste determination (261 listings + characteristics: ignitability, corrosivity, reactivity, toxicity/TCLP), use proper containers and labeling, and ship via a licensed transporter under a hazardous-waste manifest (e-Manifest). Used oil is managed under 40 CFR 279 (not counted as hazardous waste if handled per the used-oil rules). Universal wastes (batteries, lamps, certain aerosols) have streamlined 40 CFR 273 handling.
key_requirements: Make and document a hazardous-waste determination for every non-exempt waste stream (listings + characteristics/TCLP).
Know your generator category by monthly quantity — it drives accumulation time, training, and reporting.
Obtain an EPA ID number (SQG/LQG) and ship hazardous waste on a manifest via a permitted transporter/TSDF.
Meet accumulation-time limits (VSQG minimal; SQG 180/270 days; LQG 90 days) and container/labeling standards.
Manage used oil under 40 CFR 279 and universal wastes under 40 CFR 273.
forms: EPA Form 8700-12 (Notification / obtain EPA ID number)
Uniform Hazardous Waste Manifest (EPA Form 8700-22) via e-Manifest
deadlines: SQG accumulation: 180 days (270 if TSDF >200 miles)
LQG accumulation: 90 days
LQG Biennial Report: by March 1 of even-numbered years for the prior year
penalty_structure: RCRA civil penalties up to a statutory maximum per violation per day (adjusted annually for inflation); knowing violations can carry criminal liability.
failure_points: No hazardous-waste determination on shop solvents/paint/absorbents.
Misjudging generator category and blowing accumulation limits (e.g., LQG holding waste past 90 days).
Storing used oil improperly or mixing it with hazardous waste (loses the 279 used-oil status).
Shipping without an EPA ID or manifest; incomplete labels/dates on satellite/accumulation containers.
cross_refs: E&P exemption for uniquely-associated wastes (see epa-rcra-ep-exemption)
EPCRA chemical inventory for stored chemicals (see epa-epcra-tier2)
Spill reporting if a hazardous substance releases (see epa-cercla-reporting)
notes: Category thresholds verified (100 kg / 1,000 kg per month; 1 kg acute). Reference only.

title: Clean Air Act NSPS OOOO & OOOOa — Oil & Gas VOC/Methane (legacy sources)
citation: 40 CFR Part 60 Subparts OOOO & OOOOa; CAA §111(b)
applies_to: Oil & gas sources that commenced construction/modification/reconstruction after Aug 23, 2011 (OOOO) or after Sept 18, 2015 (OOOOa) and before Dec 6, 2022.
summary: NSPS OOOO (2012) and OOOOa (2016) are the earlier New Source Performance Standards for the crude oil & natural gas source category under CAA §111(b). OOOO set VOC (and some SO2) standards for equipment such as gas-well completions (green/reduced-emission completions), storage vessels, compressors, pneumatic controllers, and gas-plant equipment leaks. OOOOa expanded coverage to add methane (in addition to VOC) and imposed the first federal fugitive-emissions monitoring (LDAR) program for well sites and compressor stations using optical gas imaging (OGI) or EPA Method 21. A source's 'commence construction' date determines which subpart applies: OOOO for sources after 8/23/2011, OOOOa for sources after 9/18/2015, and the newer OOOOb for sources after 12/6/2022. OOOO/OOOOa remain in force for sources built in their windows; EPA's 2024 rule also added regulatory language clarifying when such sources transition into a state/federal plan under EG OOOOc.
key_requirements: Reduced-emission ('green') completions for hydraulically fractured gas wells.
VOC (OOOO) and VOC+methane (OOOOa) controls on storage vessels, compressors, and pneumatic controllers.
OOOOa: periodic LDAR fugitive-emissions surveys (OGI/Method 21) at well sites and compressor stations with repair timelines.
Recordkeeping and annual reporting of monitoring, repairs, and control-device performance.
deadlines: Applicability set by 'commence construction/modification' date (8/23/2011 OOOO; 9/18/2015 OOOOa)
LDAR survey frequency and repair deadlines per the applicable subpart
penalty_structure: CAA civil penalties per day per violation (inflation-adjusted); potential criminal liability for knowing violations.
failure_points: Applying the wrong subpart for the source's construction date.
Missing periodic OGI/Method 21 surveys or repair deadlines under OOOOa.
Poor storage-vessel VOC control records / uncontrolled pneumatic devices.
notes: Reference only. Which subpart applies is date-driven; confirm the source's commence-construction date.

title: Clean Air Act NSPS OOOOb — New Oil & Gas Sources (methane/VOC, 2024 rule)
citation: 40 CFR Part 60 Subpart OOOOb; CAA §111(b); 89 FR 16820 (Mar 8, 2024)
applies_to: Crude oil & natural gas facilities that commence construction, modification, or reconstruction AFTER December 6, 2022 — well sites, centralized production facilities, compressor stations, and gas processing plants.
summary: NSPS OOOOb is EPA's 2024 New Source Performance Standard (final rule published March 8, 2024; effective May 7, 2024) setting methane and VOC (and SO2 for sweetening) limits for NEW/modified/reconstructed oil & gas sources built after Dec 6, 2022. It substantially strengthens the fugitive-emissions program: for each 'fugitive emissions component' affected facility, operators must run a monitoring-and-repair (LDAR) program whose frequency and method (AVO — audible/visual/olfactory — plus OGI or Method 21) depend on the type and quantity of equipment at the site, not an emissions tonnage threshold. A fugitive emission means any AVO indication, any visible emission on an OGI instrument, or a Method 21 reading of 500 ppmv or greater; leaks must be repaired on set timelines. OOOOb phases out most routine flaring of associated gas, tightens storage-vessel and pneumatic-controller standards (zero-emission controllers as BSER in many cases), and covers pumps and compressors. It also creates a Super-Emitter Program: when EPA forwards a certified third-party detection of a release of 100 kg/hr of methane or more (satellite, aircraft, or mobile monitoring), an operator within 50 meters must investigate and, if it's their source, fix it and report. Appendix K is the standardized OGI protocol.
key_requirements: Run a fugitive-emissions monitoring & repair (LDAR) program per §60.5397b — AVO at all site types plus OGI/Method 21 at applicable site types; frequency set by equipment type/count.
Treat as a leak any AVO indication, any OGI-visible emission, or Method 21 >= 500 ppmv; repair within the required timeframe.
Eliminate routine flaring of associated gas where required; route to sales/use/control.
Use zero-emission (non-emitting) pneumatic controllers/pumps where BSER applies; control storage vessels.
Respond to Super-Emitter notifications (>=100 kg/hr methane): investigate within 50 m, mitigate, and report.
Complete well-closure surveys (OGI) and keep records/reports per §60.5420b.
forms: Electronic reports via EPA's CEDRI (annual/periodic reports under §60.5420b)
deadlines: Applies to sources commencing construction/modification/reconstruction after Dec 6, 2022
Rule effective May 7, 2024; LDAR survey frequencies and repair deadlines per subpart
Super-emitter investigation triggered on receipt of a certified EPA notification
penalty_structure: CAA §113 civil penalties per day per violation (inflation-adjusted); knowing violations can be criminal.
failure_points: Assuming a small site is exempt — monitoring is driven by equipment type/quantity, not a tonnage threshold.
Missing periodic OGI surveys or blowing repair deadlines; poor Appendix K documentation.
Continuing routine associated-gas flaring where prohibited; using emitting pneumatic controllers.
Ignoring a Super-Emitter notification for a facility within 50 m of the reported location.
source: 40 CFR 60 Subpart OOOOb; 89 FR 16820; EPA Small Entity Compliance Guide (May 2024); EPA Fugitive Emissions FAQ (Sept 2024)
notes: Facts verified: after Dec 6 2022; effective May 7 2024; 500 ppmv Method 21; 100 kg/hr super-emitter; 50 m investigation radius. EPA reconsidered narrow flare/monitoring issues (2024). Reference only.

title: Clean Air Act EG OOOOc — Emission Guidelines for EXISTING Oil & Gas Sources
citation: 40 CFR Part 60 Subpart OOOOc; CAA §111(d); 89 FR 16820 (Mar 8, 2024)
applies_to: Existing 'designated facilities' in the crude oil & natural gas source category that commenced construction/reconstruction/modification ON OR BEFORE December 6, 2022 — regulated through STATE plans (or a federal plan).
summary: EG OOOOc is the first nationwide Emission Guidelines under CAA §111(d) for EXISTING oil & gas sources, setting presumptive methane standards that STATES must translate into enforceable state plans (a federal plan applies where a state does not act). Unlike NSPS OOOOb (which applies directly to new sources), OOOOc works through state plans — so the specific obligations an existing wellsite/compressor/tank faces will come from the operator's STATE program built on EPA's presumptive standards. The presumptive standards mirror OOOOb in substance (fugitive-emissions LDAR, storage vessels, pneumatic controllers/pumps, associated-gas flaring limits, well closure) and include the same Super-Emitter Program and Appendix K OGI protocol and allowance for advanced methane-detection technologies. States were given a deadline to submit plans, after which existing sources phase into compliance on the schedule the state adopts. Origin should tell contractors: for existing equipment, watch your STATE's OOOOc plan for the exact deadlines.
key_requirements: Existing designated facilities become subject to methane standards through an EPA-approved STATE plan (or a federal plan).
Presumptive standards parallel OOOOb: LDAR fugitive monitoring, storage-vessel and pneumatic-device controls, associated-gas routing, well-closure surveys.
Super-Emitter Program (>=100 kg/hr methane) applies to existing sources via the state plan.
Compliance timing is set by the state plan, not directly by the federal rule.
deadlines: States submit §111(d) plans on EPA's schedule; existing-source compliance follows the approved state plan
Applicability cutoff: sources constructed/reconstructed/modified on or before Dec 6, 2022
penalty_structure: Enforced through the approved state (or federal) plan under CAA authority; per-day civil penalties (inflation-adjusted).
failure_points: Assuming existing sources are unregulated — they are, via the state OOOOc plan.
Watching only the federal rule and missing STATE-plan deadlines and specifics.
Overlooking that many existing tanks/controllers must be retrofitted or replaced under the plan.
cross_refs: BLM waste-prevention overlap on flaring (see blm-waste-prevention)
notes: Reference only. Existing-source obligations flow through STATE plans — always confirm the delegated state's OOOOc plan and timeline.

title: NPDES Stormwater — Construction General Permit & SWPPP (CWA §402; 40 CFR 122/450)
applies_to: Operators of construction sites that disturb 1 or more acres (or less than 1 acre if part of a larger common plan) discharging stormwater to waters of the U.S. — including pad/road/pipeline construction where not exempt.
summary: Under the Clean Water Act NPDES program, construction that disturbs one acre or more (or under an acre but part of a larger common plan of development/sale totaling an acre or more) needs stormwater-discharge permit coverage — typically under a Construction General Permit (CGP) — and must develop and implement a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) with erosion/sediment controls and good-housekeeping/pollution-prevention practices before submitting a Notice of Intent (NOI). IMPORTANT oil & gas carve-out: CWA §402(l)(2) bars EPA (and states) from requiring an NPDES permit for stormwater from oil & gas exploration, production, processing, treatment, or transmission operations that is composed ENTIRELY of uncontaminated precipitation runoff. That exemption is LOST — and a permit is required — if the stormwater discharge (1) results in a Reportable Quantity discharge for which notification was required under 40 CFR 117.21/302.6/110.6 since Nov 16, 1987, or (2) contributes to a violation of a water-quality standard, or if the runoff is contaminated by contact with raw materials, products, byproducts, or wastes. Permitting authority varies: EPA runs the CGP only in a few areas (e.g., MA, NH, NM, most Indian country, some territories) — most states (TX, etc.) run their own NPDES programs, so the STATE CGP applies. The 2022 CGP scaled chemical-storage controls to container size and requires SWPPP-referenced spill controls (an existing SPCC can satisfy those provisions if cross-referenced).
key_requirements: Obtain stormwater permit coverage (usually via a CGP NOI) BEFORE construction disturbing >=1 acre (or <1 acre in a common plan) — and develop the SWPPP first.
Implement erosion/sediment controls, natural buffers (or equivalent), and pollution-prevention/good-housekeeping practices per the CGP and 40 CFR 450 effluent limits.
Oil & gas uncontaminated-runoff exemption under §402(l)(2) applies UNLESS an RQ discharge, water-quality violation, or contact-contamination occurs.
Cross-reference an existing SPCC plan in the SWPPP to satisfy chemical spill/leak controls; scale controls to container size (<55 gal vs >=55 gal).
Confirm whether EPA or the STATE is the permitting authority and use that authority's CGP and eReporting tool (EPA's NeT for EPA-CGP areas).
forms: Notice of Intent (NOI) — via EPA NeT (EPA-CGP areas) or the state equivalent
Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) — kept on site, not filed
Notice of Termination (NOT) at project close
deadlines: SWPPP complete and NOI submitted before commencing construction
Emergency-related projects: NOI within 30 days of commencing
Routine SWPPP inspections per the CGP (e.g., after storm events)
penalty_structure: CWA §309 civil penalties per day per violation (inflation-adjusted); administrative and criminal enforcement possible.
failure_points: Assuming the oil & gas stormwater exemption is automatic — it is lost with contaminated runoff, an RQ discharge, or a water-quality violation.
Starting earthwork before securing permit coverage / writing the SWPPP.
Using the EPA CGP where the STATE is actually the permitting authority (or vice-versa).
Inadequate erosion/sediment controls, missing inspections, or no SPCC cross-reference for on-site fuel/chemicals.
cross_refs: SPCC oil-storage plan can satisfy SWPPP spill controls (see epa-spcc)
Sheen-rule reporting if a discharge occurs (see epa-oil-discharge-reporting)
State NPDES authority varies (see state_plan records)
source: CWA §402 & §402(l)(2); 40 CFR 122.26 & 450; EPA 2022 CGP & Fact Sheet; EPA Oil and Gas Stormwater Permitting FAQ
notes: Facts verified: 1-acre threshold, §402(l)(2) O&G exemption + loss conditions, EPA-CGP states (MA/NH/NM/most Indian country/territories), TX runs its own program. Reference only.

title: UIC Class II Injection Wells — Produced-Water & Enhanced-Recovery Disposal (SDWA; 40 CFR 144-147)
applies_to: Owners/operators injecting fluids associated with oil & gas production — saltwater/brine (produced water) disposal wells, enhanced-recovery wells, and hydrocarbon-storage wells.
summary: The Safe Drinking Water Act's Underground Injection Control (UIC) program regulates injection wells to prevent contamination of Underground Sources of Drinking Water (USDWs). Class II wells handle fluids from oil & gas production: Type D produced-fluid (saltwater/brine) disposal wells, Type R enhanced-recovery wells, Type H hydrocarbon-storage wells, and Type A annular-disposal. Because production generates huge volumes of brine (often saltier than seawater and containing metals/NORM), deep injection into isolated formations is the standard disposal path. Most oil & gas states have PRIMACY over Class II wells under SDWA §1425 (demonstrating their standards prevent USDW endangerment) or §1422 (meeting EPA's minimum requirements) — so the state agency (Texas RRC, New Mexico OCD, etc.) is usually the permitting authority; EPA directly implements only where a state lacks primacy. Requirements cover well construction/casing/cementing, maximum injection pressure, mechanical integrity testing (MIT), monitoring, area-of-review, recordkeeping, reporting, and plugging/closure. Disposal wells require individual permits; enhanced-recovery wells may be permitted or authorized by rule. Injecting DIESEL fuels for hydraulic fracturing requires a Class II permit first. Induced-seismicity concerns have led several states to add pressure/volume limits and monitoring near faults.
key_requirements: Obtain a UIC Class II permit (or rule authorization for eligible enhanced-recovery wells) BEFORE injecting — from the state primacy agency or EPA where EPA implements.
Meet construction/casing/cementing standards and demonstrate the well will not endanger USDWs (area-of-review analysis).
Perform periodic Mechanical Integrity Tests (MIT) and stay within permitted maximum injection pressure/volume.
Monitor, keep records, and file required injection reports; follow proper plugging & abandonment at closure.
Get a Class II permit before injecting diesel fuels for hydraulic fracturing.
Comply with any state induced-seismicity conditions (pressure/volume limits, seismic monitoring).
forms: EPA Form 7520-6 — UIC Permit Application for a Class II Well (or the state equivalent)
EPA Forms 7520-x series (MIT, annual/monitoring reports) where EPA implements
deadlines: Permit issued before injection begins; MIT and monitoring/reporting on permit schedule
Plugging/closure per permit and state rules
penalty_structure: SDWA civil penalties per day per violation (inflation-adjusted); state programs impose their own penalties and can shut in wells.
failure_points: Injecting before permit issuance or exceeding permitted pressure/volume.
Missed or failed Mechanical Integrity Tests.
Injecting diesel for frac without a Class II permit.
Ignoring induced-seismicity permit conditions; improper plugging at closure.
cross_refs: Produced water is largely RCRA-exempt but still regulated here (see epa-rcra-ep-exemption)
BLM produced-water handling on Federal leases (see blm-produced-water)
source: SDWA §1421/1422/1425; 40 CFR 144-147; epa.gov Class II Oil and Gas Related Injection Wells; EPA Form 7520-6
notes: Facts verified: Class II types A/D/H/R, §1422 vs §1425 primacy, Form 7520-6, diesel-frac permit requirement. Most O&G states have primacy. Reference only.

title: EPCRA Sections 311/312 — SDS & Tier II Chemical Inventory (40 CFR 370)
applies_to: Facilities required to keep OSHA Safety Data Sheets that store hazardous chemicals at or above reporting thresholds — including yards, shops, and production facilities with fuel, chemicals, and EHSs.
summary: The Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act (EPCRA) gives responders and communities information about on-site chemicals. Section 311 requires a facility that must maintain OSHA Safety Data Sheets (SDS) to submit those SDSs (or a list) to the State/Tribal Emergency Response Commission (SERC/TERC), Local/Tribal Emergency Planning Committee (LEPC/TEPC), and the local fire department — a one-time submission within 30 days of first exceeding a threshold, updated on significant changes. Section 312 then requires an ANNUAL Emergency and Hazardous Chemical Inventory (the Tier II form) to the same three recipients by MARCH 1 each year, covering the prior calendar year. Reporting thresholds (40 CFR 370.10): Extremely Hazardous Substances (EHSs, listed in 40 CFR 355) at 500 pounds OR their Threshold Planning Quantity, whichever is LOWER; all other OSHA hazardous chemicals at 10,000 pounds; special retail-fuel thresholds of 75,000 gallons (gasoline) and 100,000 gallons (diesel) for compliant USTs. Tier II reports storage amounts in range codes, storage type/conditions, and locations. States often set LOWER thresholds and their own e-filing systems (e.g., Texas Tier II via TCEQ/Texas STEPS). EPCRA §302 emergency planning is separately triggered when an EHS is on site at or above its TPQ.
key_requirements: Submit SDSs or a chemical list under §311 to SERC/LEPC/fire department within 30 days of first exceeding a threshold (one-time, update on changes).
File the annual Tier II inventory under §312 by MARCH 1 to SERC/TERC, LEPC/TEPC, and the local fire department for the prior calendar year.
Apply thresholds: EHS = 500 lb or TPQ (whichever lower); all other hazardous chemicals = 10,000 lb; retail gasoline 75,000 gal / diesel 100,000 gal (compliant USTs).
Report each chemical's max/average amount (range codes), storage type/conditions, and location on the Tier II form.
Check STATE thresholds and filing systems — many are lower and require electronic submission plus fees.
If an EHS is present at/above its TPQ, comply with §302 emergency-planning notification too.
forms: EPA Tier II Form (or state e-filing system, e.g., Tier2 Submit / state portal)
deadlines: §312 Tier II: annually by March 1 for the prior calendar year
§311 SDS/list: within 30 days of first exceeding a threshold
§302 EHS notification: within 60 days of first having an EHS at/above its TPQ
penalty_structure: EPCRA civil penalties up to a statutory maximum per violation per day (inflation-adjusted); §325 provides administrative, civil, and criminal enforcement.
failure_points: Missing the March 1 Tier II deadline or filing with only one of the three required recipients.
Using the federal 10,000-lb threshold when the STATE threshold is lower.
Overlooking EHSs (500 lb / TPQ) — diesel/fuel and small quantities of listed EHSs can trigger reporting.
Not filing §311 SDS submissions or updating them after adding chemicals.
cross_refs: Ties to OSHA HazCom SDS program (see hazcom-related program records)
Spill of a listed substance triggers reporting (see epa-cercla-reporting)
source: EPCRA §311/§312; 40 CFR 370.10; EPA Tier II Form Instructions (2026/2027); EPCRA General Reporting Guidance
notes: Thresholds verified: EHS 500 lb/TPQ, 10,000 lb general, 75,000 gal gasoline / 100,000 gal diesel (retail USTs), March 1 annual. States often stricter. Reference only.

title: EPCRA Section 313 — Toxic Release Inventory (TRI / Form R, 40 CFR 372)
applies_to: Facilities in covered NAICS sectors with 10+ full-time-equivalent employees that manufacture, process, or otherwise use a listed TRI chemical above threshold. Historically much of upstream oil & gas production was NOT a covered sector; natural-gas processing was added to TRI reporting.
summary: The Toxic Release Inventory (TRI) under EPCRA §313 requires covered facilities to report annual releases and other waste management of listed toxic chemicals, giving the public a picture of chemical releases to air, water, and land. A facility must report if it (1) is in a covered NAICS sector, (2) employs the equivalent of 10 or more full-time employees, and (3) manufactures/processes 25,000 lb or otherwise uses 10,000 lb of a listed chemical in the year (much lower thresholds apply to PBT chemicals like lead, mercury, dioxins, and PFAS). Reports (Form R, or the shorter Form A certification for low-volume cases) are due JULY 1 for the prior calendar year via EPA's TRI-MEweb. For oil & gas: upstream extraction/production has historically fallen OUTSIDE the covered TRI sector list, but NATURAL GAS PROCESSING facilities were added as a covered sector, so gas plants must evaluate TRI applicability; midstream/downstream and certain support facilities may also be covered. Because coverage is sector- and threshold-specific, Origin should have contractors confirm their NAICS and chemical usage rather than assume they are exempt.
key_requirements: Determine TRI applicability by covered NAICS sector + 10-FTE employee test + chemical activity thresholds.
Thresholds: 25,000 lb manufactured/processed or 10,000 lb otherwise used per listed chemical (far lower for PBT/PFAS chemicals).
File Form R (or Form A where eligible) by JULY 1 for the prior calendar year via TRI-MEweb.
Natural gas processing is a COVERED sector — gas plants must evaluate reporting; upstream production historically is not covered.
Track PFAS additions to the TRI list, which carry low reporting thresholds.
forms: EPA Form R (Toxic Chemical Release Inventory Reporting Form) via TRI-MEweb
EPA Form A (Alternate Threshold Certification) where eligible
deadlines: TRI reports due July 1 for the prior calendar year
penalty_structure: EPCRA §325 civil penalties up to a statutory maximum per violation per day (inflation-adjusted).
failure_points: Gas-processing facilities assuming the historic upstream exemption applies to them — processing is a covered sector.
Missing the July 1 deadline or failing to count 'otherwise use' quantities.
Overlooking low PBT/PFAS thresholds.
Miscounting FTE hours across a multi-crew operation.
cross_refs: Tier II inventory is a separate EPCRA obligation (see epa-epcra-tier2)
source: EPCRA §313; 40 CFR 372; epa.gov TRI program; TRI covered-sectors guidance
notes: Reference only. TRI coverage is sector/threshold specific — natural gas processing is covered; confirm NAICS + chemical volumes. PFAS additions carry low thresholds.

title: CERCLA Hazardous-Substance Release Reporting — Reportable Quantities (40 CFR 302)
applies_to: Any person in charge of a vessel or facility from which a CERCLA hazardous substance is released to the environment at or above its Reportable Quantity in a 24-hour period.
summary: Under CERCLA (Superfund) §103, the person in charge of a facility must IMMEDIATELY notify the National Response Center (1-800-424-8802) whenever a listed hazardous substance is released to the environment in an amount at or above its Reportable Quantity (RQ) within any 24-hour period, unless the release is federally permitted. About 800 hazardous substances (drawn from CWA §311, CWA §307(a), CAA §112, and RCRA §3001) have assigned RQs listed in 40 CFR 302.4, Table 302.4 (RQs of 1, 10, 100, 1,000, or 5,000 lb). This is separate from — and often in addition to — the oil 'sheen rule' (which covers oil, not CERCLA hazardous substances) and EPCRA §304 (which requires parallel notice to the SERC/LEPC for releases of CERCLA hazardous substances and EPCRA EHSs that could expose people off-site). Common oil-field substances with low RQs include hydrogen sulfide, benzene, and certain glycols/acids. A continuous, stable release may qualify for reduced 'continuous release' reporting under 40 CFR 302.8 after initial notifications.
key_requirements: Immediately notify the NRC (1-800-424-8802) for any release of a CERCLA hazardous substance at or above its RQ in 24 hours (unless federally permitted).
Also give EPCRA §304 notice to the SERC/TERC and LEPC/TEPC for releases with potential off-site exposure.
Know low-RQ field chemicals (e.g., H2S, benzene) and follow state release-reporting rules too.
Use the 'continuous release' provisions (302.8) only after required initial notifications.
forms: Telephonic NRC notification; EPCRA §304 follow-up written notice to SERC/LEPC
deadlines: NRC and §304 notifications: immediately upon knowledge of an RQ release
EPCRA §304 written follow-up notice as soon as practicable
penalty_structure: CERCLA §103 and EPCRA §325 civil and criminal penalties for failure to notify (inflation-adjusted per-day amounts).
failure_points: Reporting an oil sheen but missing a co-released hazardous substance over its RQ (e.g., H2S/benzene).
Calling NRC but skipping the EPCRA §304 SERC/LEPC notice.
Not knowing the low RQs for common field chemicals.
Assuming a permitted air/water release covers an unpermitted spill.
cross_refs: Oil sheen-rule reporting for oil (see epa-oil-discharge-reporting)
EPCRA inventory of the same chemicals (see epa-epcra-tier2)
source: CERCLA §103; 40 CFR 302.4/302.6/302.8; epa.gov Hazardous Substance Designations and Release Notifications
notes: NRC 1-800-424-8802 verified; ~800 substances; RQ tiers 1/10/100/1,000/5,000 lb. Reference only — never enters send-gate.

title: Oil Pollution Act — Facility Response Plans & FRP Facilities (40 CFR 112.20)
citation: Oil Pollution Act of 1990; CWA §311(j)(5); 40 CFR 112.20-112.21
applies_to: SPCC-regulated facilities that, because of their location and oil-storage volume, could cause 'substantial harm' to the environment by discharging oil into navigable waters — a subset of larger onshore oil facilities.
summary: The Oil Pollution Act of 1990 (enacted after the Exxon Valdez spill) added CWA §311(j)(5), under which certain 'substantial harm' facilities must prepare and submit a Facility Response Plan (FRP) — a more demanding plan than SPCC, focused on RESPONDING to a worst-case oil discharge. A facility is an FRP facility if it is subject to SPCC and meets the 'substantial harm' criteria in 40 CFR 112.20 — generally: total oil storage capacity of 1 million gallons or more AND a location/condition factor (e.g., inability to contain a worst-case discharge, proximity to fish/wildlife or public drinking-water intakes, or a spill history), OR any facility EPA designates. FRPs must identify a worst-case discharge scenario, ensure response resources and trained personnel are available, establish notification and response procedures, and be reviewed/updated and re-submitted on set cycles and after material changes. Most small oil-field contractors are NOT FRP facilities, but large tank farms, terminals, and central facilities can be. FRP is layered on top of — not instead of — SPCC.
key_requirements: Determine 'substantial harm' status under 40 CFR 112.20 (generally >=1,000,000 gal oil capacity + a location/harm factor, or EPA designation).
If an FRP facility, prepare and SUBMIT a Facility Response Plan to EPA (unlike the SPCC, which is not filed).
Plan for a worst-case discharge: response resources, contracted responders (OSRO), notification chains, and trained/drilled personnel.
Conduct response drills/exercises and review/update the FRP on the required cycle and after material changes.
Maintain the underlying SPCC Plan as well — FRP does not replace SPCC.
forms: Facility Response Plan (submitted to the EPA Regional Administrator; 40 CFR 112 Appendices)
deadlines: FRP submitted before operating as a substantial-harm facility; periodic review/resubmission and post-change updates
penalty_structure: CWA §311 civil/administrative penalties for failure to prepare/submit/implement an FRP; OPA liability for removal costs and damages.
failure_points: Missing FRP applicability at a large central facility/tank farm (>=1M gal + harm factor).
Treating the SPCC as sufficient when an FRP is also required.
No worst-case-discharge planning, response contracts, or drills.
Failing to resubmit after capacity/location changes.
source: OPA 1990; CWA §311(j)(5); 40 CFR 112.20-112.21; epa.gov FRP program
notes: Reference only. Substantial-harm threshold generally 1,000,000 gal + a location/harm factor; small contractors usually exempt but large facilities are not.

title: EPA Program Delegation to States — Who Actually Permits Oil & Gas Environmental Work
agency: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and authorized state agencies
applies_to: Every oil & gas contractor — because the day-to-day permitting authority for most EPA programs is a delegated STATE agency, not federal EPA.
summary: A recurring theme across EPA programs: Congress designed most of them to be delegated to the states, so once EPA approves a state program, the STATE agency issues permits, inspects, and enforces under rules that must be at least as stringent as the federal floor (and are often stricter). For an oil & gas contractor this means: NPDES stormwater and discharge permits usually come from the state (e.g., TCEQ in Texas) except in the few EPA-CGP areas (MA, NH, NM, most Indian country, certain territories); UIC Class II injection is run by state primacy agencies (Texas Railroad Commission, New Mexico OCD, etc.) in nearly all oil states; RCRA hazardous-waste programs are state-run in most states; and CAA methane standards reach existing sources through STATE §111(d) plans under EG OOOOc. Federal EPA directly implements only where a state lacks authorization, plus on many tribal/Indian lands. Practical rule Origin should give contractors: find your delegated state agency FIRST, because that is who you file with and who inspects you — but know the federal rule sets the minimum and tribal/federal lands may fall to EPA or BLM. This mirrors (and complements) the OSHA state-plan divergence layer.
key_requirements: Identify the delegated STATE agency for each program (air, water/NPDES, UIC, RCRA) before assuming federal EPA is the authority.
Treat federal EPA rules as the FLOOR — states may impose stricter limits, lower thresholds, and extra reporting.
On tribal/Indian and some federal lands, EPA (or BLM) may directly implement instead of the state.
Confirm which authority runs the CGP, the UIC program, and the §111(d) methane plan in the operating state.
cross_refs: Existing-source methane via state plans (see epa-eg-ooooc)
Parallels OSHA state-plan divergence (see state_plan records)
source: CAA §111(d); CWA §402; RCRA §3006; SDWA §1422/1425; epa.gov delegation/primacy pages
notes: Reference only. Orientation record so Origin always points contractors to the correct (usually state) permitting authority.
